# A novel fibronectin-binding peptide reveals dynamic intermediate structures during matrix assembly

Henry A. Resnikoff, Aaron J. Hamlin, Faith M. Reash, Emily N. Sabatino, Isabella M. Strumolo, Luqiong Wang & Jean E. Schwarzbauer

The extracellular matrix (ECM) is an expansive network of polymers that regulates cell adhesion, migration, and tissue morphogenesis, and that becomes dysregulated in fibrotic disease states. Of the many ECM proteins, fibronectin (FN) is foundational and FN fibrils are instrumental in promoting deposition of many other ECM proteins. FN fibrils form by cell receptor-mediated polymerization of secreted FN dimers. To provide a deeper understanding of the FN assembly process, we sought to identify FN-binding peptides that could be used to target FN during matrix assembly. Here we report the isolation of a FN-binding peptide, S2, by M13 phage display. When displayed within a GST-S2- EGFP fusion protein, S2 directs incorporation of the fluorescent fusion protein into FN fibrils during fibroblast matrix assembly, enabling direct visualization of fibril formation and accumulation. The S2 fusion protein remains stably associated with FN in decellularized matrices. Live cell imaging with GST-S2-EGFP revealed events in matrix formation and maturation and highlighted distinct features of FN assembly such as nascent fibril nucleation and elongation from coalescing FN aggregates. This S2 peptide fusion protein represents a new tool for real-time analysis of the ECM, for generation of fluorescent scaffolds, and for directing functional proteins to FN matrix.

Keywords  Fibronectin, Extracellular matrix, Phage display, Matrix assembly, GFP fusion protein, Liveimaging

Fibronectin (FN) is a foundational extracellular matrix (ECM) molecule that plays essential roles in cell adhesion, migration, and differentiation1. It serves as a scaffold for cells and other ECM proteins, influencing tissue organization and cellular signaling2–4. FN is essential for embryonic development5 and plays key roles in tissue morphogenesis6–8. Dysregulation of FN assembly has been implicated in a wide range of pathological conditions including fibrosis9–12, cancer13,14, skeletal abnormalities15,16 and cardiovascular disease17.

FN exists as a large glycoprotein composed of multiple functional domains that facilitate interactions with integrins, growth factors, and other ECM molecules18,19. It is secreted as a soluble dimer and undergoes fibrillogenesis, a process driven by cell-FN interactions that converts soluble FN into insoluble fibrils4,19. This dynamic assembly is crucial for ECM deposition and organization. Despite its importance, visualizing FN matrix formation in live-cell systems remains a technical challenge, limiting our ability to study its real-time dynamics and cellular interactions.

Traditional methods for studying FN matrix include immunofluorescence staining and addition or expression of fluorescently-tagged proteins. While these approaches provide valuable insights, they each have drawbacks for studying ECM dynamics. For example, immunofluorescence staining often requires fixation, which halts the assembly process, whereas genetically-tagged ECM proteins limit study of FN to the organisms/cells in which the tag exists. Addition of fluorescently-tagged FN to cell cultures marks sites where assembly is occurring but may give incomplete labeling that may bias analysis. As such, a probe that could be deployed in diverse systems and allow for live imaging of FN would facilitate analysis of FN matrix assembly and help further our understanding of FN in both healthy and pathological contexts.

Adherent cultured cells such as fibroblasts or endothelial cells deposit FN-rich matrices that mimic aspects of tissue microenvironments. These and other in vitro models have been instrumental in understanding FN’s role in physiological and pathological conditions. To address this goal, we leveraged phage display technology to develop a novel GFP-tagged FN-binding protein that integrates into FN fibrils. We identified a unique peptide that allows for live imaging of FN matrix formation and offers the unique advantage of matrix retention after decellularization, enabling the study of fluorescent FN matrices in both culture systems and cell-derived scaffolds. Here, we describe the development and application of this tool for visualizing FN matrix dynamics in both fixed and live-cell environments.

Results Identification of FN-binding peptides using phage display We screened an M13 phage display library for peptides that bind to a recombinant N-terminal 70 kDa fragment of human FN. The 70 kDa fragment is composed of two domains, the assembly domain with the FN-binding site that is required for matrix assembly and the gelatin/collagen-binding domain (Supplementary Figure S1). The phage display library displaying 12 amino acid-long peptides was panned against plates coated with the 70 kDa fragment following the workflow in Supplementary Figure S1. After 3 rounds of panning, 47 phages were randomly selected for sequencing, which yielded 26 unique peptide sequences. 11 of the 26 sequences were found in multiple phage isolates (Fig. 1A). Binding of individual phage clones to 70 kDa was confirmed with an enzyme linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), using pooled unbound phage from the first pan as a negative control. All but 2 of the 26 unique sequences generated a positive ELISA signal, as defined by a mean signal higher than 3x the average negative control signal (Fig. 1A).

Phage binding was scored as positive if phage signal both resembled and overlayed the fibrillar structure of the FN matrix (Fig. 1B, Supplementary Figure S2). Three of the phage clones (S2, S12, S39) exhibited a fibrillar pattern with extensive colocalization with the FN matrix. The observation that most of the peptides did not bind to FN fibrils after assembly and fixation suggests that the binding sites might not be accessible or may be affected by fixation. Phage clones were incubated with growing fibroblast cultures during matrix assembly for 48 h followed by fixation and staining. Since our phage display screening was against human 70 kDa, we used human WI-38 fibroblasts in this experiment to assess incorporation of phage into FN matrix. As with the matrix binding experiment with mouse cells, phages with peptide S2, S12, or S39 showed significant incorporation into the human FN matrix (Fig. 2A). The WT negative control phage showed very little association with FN fibrils. In contrast to the binding results, a number of phage peptides showed signal above background in the incorporation experiment, such as S37 phage (Fig. 2). To quantify the relationship between FN and phage signals, we generated Pearson’s correlation coefficients, which measure how closely pixel intensities in one channel correlate with those in the other (range − 1 to + 1). Values near + 1 indicate strong positive colocalization, 0 indicates no linear relationship, and − 1 indicates inverse correlation. Only 4 of the phage signals had Pearson’s coefficients higher than 0.5. S2, S12, and S39 had the highest coefficients (0.70, 0.61, 0.57, respectively; Fig. 2B). S37 was also higher than the others (0.53). However, most of the phages had coefficients below 0.5 indicating limited fibril-phage overlap.

Differences between phage in their colocalizations with FN signals could result from concentration differences between amplified phage stocks. We decided to create high concentration phage stocks for the two phages with the highest Pearson’s coefficients, S2 and S12, to see if there was a dose-dependent effect. Incubation with a 10-fold higher concentration of S2 phage gave essentially complete coverage of fibrils by phage (Fig. 3A-C, G) while S12 phage gave increased coverage but also showed an increase in punctate background signal (Fig. 3D-F). The Pearson’s coefficient for S2 (0.82) was also increased, while the Pearson’s coefficient for S12 did not indicate greater colocalization with more concentrated phage (0.55). Altogether, we conclude that the S2 phage gives highly co-localized FN fibril labeling compared to the other peptides. This conclusion is further supported by confocal images depicting a single fibril within an NIH 3T3-derived ECM in which there is significant overlap between phage and FN signals (Fig. 3G, H, I).

Generation and testing of a peptide-EGFP fusion protein Phage clones were useful for characterizing peptide-FN binding activities and confirming FN fibril localization. However, there is an upper limit to the phage concentrations that can be easily generated and for some experiments, increasing the phage concentration led to higher background staining. Therefore, we decided to create a peptide fusion protein. We selected the pGEX4T3-GST-EGFP expression plasmid, into which the peptide cDNA was inserted between glutathione-S-transferase (GST) and green fluorescent protein (EGFP) sequences yielding the GST-S2-EGFP fusion protein (Fig. 4A). A tobacco etch virus (TEV) protease cleavage site lies between GST and the peptide, enabling removal of the GST tag. Thus, the peptide fusion protein can be purified via the GST tag and subsequently cleaved to produce a peptide-EGFP protein.

We tested the S2 fusion protein by adding it to fibroblast cultures to determine if it behaved similarly to the peptide-phage. We found that full-length GST-S2-EGFP fusion protein was incorporated into FN fibrils during assembly and showed significant overlap with FN immunostaining following fixation (Fig. 4A). A GST-S2- mScarlet fusion protein gave essentially the same FN binding and matrix incorporation results as GST-S2-EGFP. The specificity of GST-S2-EGFP for FN was shown with a solid phase binding assay. The fusion protein bound to the N-terminal 70 kDa fragment and to full length FN, but did not bind to other FN fragments or to other ECM proteins (laminin-111, fibrinogen, and type I collagen) (Supplementary Figure S3). The GST-Control- EGFP fusion protein did not associate with FN fibrils (Fig. 4B) indicating that the association is not due to the fusion partners. The GST tag was cleaved to yield S2-EGFP, but cultures incubated with this truncated fusion protein showed no fluorescent signal (Fig. 4C). We also found no S2-EGFP incorporation after incubation with an equimolar mixture of GST and S2-EGFP proteins (not shown). We conclude that the cleaved fusion protein is unable to be incorporated into FN fibrils. A fusion protein was generated using peptide S3, which supported phage binding to 70 kDa in a solid phase assay (Fig. 1A) but only weak association with FN matrix (Fig. 2B). GST-S3-EGFP showed no detectable FN fibril binding in culture (Fig. 4D). Together, these data demonstrate that the S2 peptide is necessary for binding of GST-S2-EGFP to FN fibrils and that binding is mediated by interaction between GST-S2-EGFP and the N-terminal 70 kDa aspect of FN.

To determine whether there is a correlation between FN matrix levels and amount of associated S2 fusion protein, we used normal human lung fibroblasts (NHLFs), which substantially increase FN matrix assembly upon treatment with TGFß11. Cells were treated or not with TGFß during 3 days of growth to generate cultures with different levels of FN matrix. Cell lysates were collected and examined by immunoblotting (Supplementary Figure S4). To allow the calculation of the mass of each protein in the lysates, known masses of GST-S2-EGFP and FN were included on the immunoblots. Lysates from untreated cells contained approximately 3 nmol of FN and 0.16 nmol of GST-S2-EGFP, showing sub-stoichiometric levels of the S2 fusion protein relative to FN. TGFß induced a significant 5-fold increase in FN to ~ 16 nmol total. GST-S2-EGFP also increased in the TGFß lysates by 2.5-fold to approximately 0.4 nmol. Thus both proteins are increased with TGFß treatment, albeit not to the same proportion.

GST-S2-EGFP stably colocalizes with FN fibrils in decellularized ECM After demonstrating that GST-S2-EGFP colocalizes with FN fibrils in growing cell cultures, we tested the stability of its association using decellularized matrices produced by NIH 3T3 fibroblasts. Cells were cultured under our standard conditions for decellularization supplemented with 2.5 µg/mL GST-S2-EGFP and were then decellularized with NP-40 detergent, low salt, high pH buffers23. After decellularization, matrices were stored in PBS at 4 ˚C and, after varying periods of time, GST-S2-EGFP association with FN fibrils was assessed.

Discussion Fibronectin (FN) matrix assembly plays a central role in tissue morphogenesis and disease and facilitates the deposition and organization of other ECM components. FN fibrillogenesis is a dynamic assembly process that depends on cell-FN and FN-FN interactions to yield a fibrillar network. Fully understanding this process requires visualizing assembly in live-cell systems. In this study, we identified a 12-amino acid peptide, S2, that enables fluorescent labeling of FN matrix in both live and fixed cell systems. The S2 peptide derived from an M13 phage display library panned against the 70 kDa N-terminal FN fragment outperformed other peptide candidates in promoting phage binding to matrix and incorporation into FN fibrils. Surprisingly, when displayed within the GST-S2-EGFP fusion protein, but not within the cleaved S2-EGFP construct, the peptide directs fusion protein incorporation into FN fibrils thus generating a fluorescent FN matrix. In cultures of both human and mouse cells, GST-S2-EGFP rapidly bound to preexisting FN matrix, was incorporated into newly assembled fibrils, and remained stably associated with insoluble FN matrix over time. Beyond enabling generation of fluorescent ECM, the S2 fusion protein permitted live imaging of ECM formation, revealing intermediate structures in the progression of FN fibril nucleation, elongation, accumulation, and remodeling over time. Given its versatility, S2-based proteins could be applied across cell culture systems to detect ECM alterations arising from diverse perturbations including drug treatment, mechanical stress, or disease-associated mutations.

Live-cell imaging with GST-S2-EGFP revealed that FN matrix accumulation occurred preferentially in regions of high cell density, and that early deposition of nascent fibrils promoted subsequent regional matrix growth. At higher magnification, we observed cells consolidating punctate FN structures into fibrils and elongating globular aggregates into fibrillar forms. These observations showcase that FN fibrillogenesis can proceed through the maturation of pre-deposited intermediates, in which punctate or small globular deposits are remodeled into fibrils by cells. The reorganization of these pre-deposited structures into fibrillar networks indicates that early stages of FN matrix are not static but remain highly dynamic, a feature that is difficult to observe with fixed samples. Astrof and colleagues20 used single-molecule imaging to show fibrils composed of FN nanodomains in linear arrays. It is possible that our small FN aggregates represent phase-like condensations of FN molecules at the cell surface, forming dynamic, liquid-like intermediates that subsequently stabilize into fibrils. Phase separation has been noted to be a driver of assembly of other ECM proteins25. The plasticity of early FN assembly emphasizes that FN matrix organization is a dynamic continuum rather than a binary state of ‘fibrils’ versus ‘non-fibrils.’ Such remodeling is likely critical for tissue homeostasis and could be dysregulated in disease contexts. We furthermore saw rearrangements of FN structures prior to and throughout cell division, highlighting how this fusion protein may uncover new aspects of cell–matrix dynamics.

Interestingly, while the N-terminal location of the S2 peptide in the phage-displayed context was sufficient for matrix binding, N-terminal exposure of the S2 peptide in the fusion protein by removal of the GST moiety completely ablated binding to FN fibrils. Each phage displays 5 copies of the peptide-coat protein fusion clustered on its surface. It is possible that dimerization of GST26,27 may enhance fusion protein binding by presenting multiple S2 copies in close proximity, as in the phage. It is also possible that proteins flanking the peptide support conformational restrictions on the peptide sequence that promote stable FN interactions. Although the precise requirements remain unclear, both the S2-phage and the S2 fusion protein were readily incorporated into FN fibrils, suggesting the constraints on S2-mediated binding are not stringent. In terms of sequence homology, NCBI BLAST analysis of the S2 peptide found only short segments of 5 or fewer amino acids with homology to human proteins. The full 12-amino acid sequence does not exist natively in the human proteome, supporting the idea that S2 is a unique sequence that likely mediates a novel mode of FN recognition.

GST-S2-EGFP offers several advantages for investigating the FN matrix. It is applicable to virtually all mammalian in vitro model systems without genetic manipulation, and labels endogenously-produced FN without further intervention. Unlike addition of exogenous FN, which can substantially affect matrix assembly, the S2 fusion protein does not change FN concentration. It is detectable both in live experiments and in fixed samples, both visually via fluorophores and biochemically. Its incorporation is robust and survives decellularization to generate fluorescent FN matrices, which may be useful tools in their own right. Others have identified FN binding peptides and used them to identify important properties of FN fibrils21,22. Although other FN-binding peptides have been described, none have been shown to drive the incorporation of a larger protein (~ 50 kDa in our case) into assembling FN fibrils or to persist within insoluble matrix through decellularization. Thus the S2 peptide reveals biochemical and functional properties not achieved by previously reported FN-binding reagents.

The modularity of the S2 fusion protein further expands its potential utility, allowing production of versions with different fluorescent moieties. Importantly, we have found that the S2 fusion protein can be added to without affecting matrix binding. Specifically, we fused the 27 kDa BioID2 enzyme onto the C-terminus of GST-S2-EGFP and successfully targeted the resulting ~ 75 kDa protein to FN matrix. This proof-of-principle construct illustrates that targeting a variety of functions to the FN matrix may be possible, such as alternative fluorescent proteins for multiplexed ECM imaging, enzymes to modify or define the ECM directly, or additional ECM proteins to alter matrix composition.

FN is upregulated in many pathological contexts—including fibrosis and cancer—where it contributes to disease progression10,11,13,28. We found that TGFβ stimulation of human lung fibroblasts increased both FN and GST-S2-EGFP deposition. TGFβ is often used in cell culture models to simulate fibrotic disease states29 and is a well-known instigator of fibrosis in vivo30. Our results open the possibility that S2-guided molecules may also concentrate at sites of fibrosis in vivo, making such a molecule useful as a diagnostic imaging agent for FN-rich lesions or as a delivery platform for therapeutics targeting fibrotic or tumor-associated ECM.

In summary, the S2 fusion protein forms specific, strong, and durable interactions with FN matrix fibrils. We believe it shows immediate promise as a versatile tool to investigate and to modify the ECM in experimental settings and shows potential as a therapeutic delivery system to FN-rich disease contexts as well.

Methods Preparation of 70 kDa FN fragment Human 70 kDa cDNA was cloned into pMAX expression vector (Addgene) between a CMV promotor and SV40 poly(A) tail sequence. The pMAX backbone also contains a kanamycin resistance gene for selection. The pMAX-70 kDa plasmid was transfected into HEK293 cells using a Lipofectamine 3000 protocol (Invitrogen), transfectants were selected with G418 (ThermoFisher) and conditioned medium of clones was screened by immunoblotting with R457 rabbit antiserum raised in-house against 70 kDa protein. HEK293 cells were grown in Minimal Essential Medium plus 10% fetal bovine serum (Hyclone) and antibiotic/antimycotic cocktail. Human plasma FN was purified from fresh-frozen plasma (Innovative Research Inc) and 70 kDa protein was purified from HEK293 cell conditioned medium by gelatin-Sepharose affinity chromatography. Proteins were > 95% pure by Coomassie blue staining after SDS-PAGE and were stored at – 80˚C in 10 mM CAPS, pH 11, 150 mM NaCl (CAPS buffer).

Phage display screening and ELISA The NEB PhD 12 library (New England Biolabs, NEB) was used with 70 kDa in a surface panning procedure following manufacturer instructions. A sterile polystyrene Petri dish was coated with a 25  µg/mL solution of 70 kDa in CAPS buffer overnight at 4˚C followed by blocking with BSA and washing with wash buffer as recommended. A 100-fold representation of the library (2 × 1011 pfu/mL) in wash buffer was incubated with the 70 kDa-coated dish for 20 min at room temperature with gentle rocking. After washing 10 times with wash buffer, bound phages were eluted with elution buffer (0.2 M glycine-HCl, pH 2.2, 1 mg/mL BSA) and neutralized with 1 M Tris-HCl, pH 9.1. Eluted phages were amplified with E. coli strain ER2738 and prepared for a second round of panning as recommended. Two subsequent rounds of panning were conducted. The final elution from the third round of panning was used to infect E. coli without amplification and 50 individual phage plaques were selected and amplified for DNA sequencing using provided primers flanking the insert region. ELISAs were conducted as recommended by NEB. # Identification of a fibronectin-binding protein signature associated with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis

**Authors:** Yu Sun; Benjamin King; Aaron J. Hamlin; Mersedeh Saniepay; Kirill Gorshkov; Gregory Barker; Milinda Ziegler; Shilpaa Mukundan; Mary Ellen Cvijic; Jean E. Schwarzbauer

**Affiliations:** 1Department of Molecular Biology, Princeton University, Princeton, New Jersey, USA 08544 | 2Leads Discovery and Optimization, Bristol Myers Squibb, Lawrenceville, New Jersey, USA 08648.

## Abstract

The extracellular matrix (ECM) is a critical component of tissue where it provides structural and signaling support to cells. Its dysregulation and accumulation lead to fibrosis, a major clinical challenge underlying many diseases that currently has little effective treatment. An understanding of the key molecular initiators of fibrosis would be both diagnostically useful and provide potential targets for therapeutics. The ECM protein fibronectin (FN) is upregulated in fibrotic conditions and other ECM proteins depend on assembly of a FN foundational ECM for their matrix incorporation. We used cell culture and in vivo models to investigate the role of FN in the progression of lung fibrosis. We confirmed that normal human lung fibroblasts (NHLFs) treated with transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-β) to stimulate fibrotic gene expression significantly increased both FN expression and its assembly into a matrix. We found that levels of alternatively spliced EDA and EDB exons were proportional to the increase in total FN RNA and protein showing that inclusion of these exons is not enhanced by TGF-β stimulation. RNA-sequencing identified 43 core matrisome genes that were significantly up- or down-regulated by TGF-β treatment and a Luminex immunoassay demonstrated increased levels of ECM proteins in conditioned medium of TGF-β-treated NHLFs. Interestingly, among the regulated core matrisome genes, 16 encode known FN-binding proteins and, of these, insulin-like growth factor binding protein 3 (IGFBP3) was most highly up-regulated. To link the NHLF results with in vivo disease, we analyzed lung tissue and bronchoalveolar lavage fluid from bleomycin-treated mice and found dramatically higher levels of FN and the FN-binding proteins IGFBP3, tenascin-C, and type I collagen in fibrotic conditions compared to controls. Altogether, our data identify a set of FN-binding proteins whose upregulation is characteristic of IPF and suggest that FN provides the foundational matrix for deposition of these proteins as fibrosis develops.

## Introduction

Fibrosis is the accumulation of extracellular matrix (ECM) proteins in insoluble and disorganized deposits within tissues that are distinct from the well-organized fibrillar networks and linear fibers that make up normal interstitial ECM [1,2]. Fibrotic deposits perturb tissue and organ functions changing cell growth and survival, adhesion, and gene expression of resident cells. The development of both normal tissues and fibrotic deposits depends on the assembly of ECM proteins into polymers. The ECM protein fibronectin (FN) is the foundational component of this assembly process and FN matrix fibrils are required to provide a scaffold for assembly of other ECM proteins, in particular, collagens [3-6]. FN polymers are key components in numerous biological functions including blood clot and provisional matrix formation in wound healing, cell invasion in pathogenesis, cell adhesion and migration required for organization of cells into tissues and organs, and by providing environmental cues for tissue resident cells as well as immune and inflammatory cells [7].

Many events that occur in fibrosis have been attributed to increased signaling by TGF-β family members [8]. FN, collagens, and their receptors along with other molecules involved in ECM formation and cell contractility are well-known to be up-regulated by TGF-β. Other mechanisms have been linked to excess ECM deposition including activation of intracellular pathways that stimulate receptors to assemble more ECM [9,10]. Because FN fibrils are central to the initiation of matrix assembly, FN levels and the formation of FN fibrils may have a critical role in the development of fibrosis and progression of disease. In that regard, degradation products of FN have been proposed as a biomarker of pulmonary fibrosis [11]. Pharmacological inhibition of FN fibrillogenesis has been reported to mitigate tissue fibrosis in an animal model [12] and FN1 does show up in comprehensive proteomic profiling of lung injury [13]. However, it is still poorly understood how FN is dysregulated and whether measurements of total FN levels or of FN matrix are useful for disease prognosis and/or diagnosis. To investigate FN’s role in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF), we used both cell culture and in vivo models, namely, TGF-β-treated normal and diseased human lung fibroblasts and a bleomycin-treated mouse model [14], respectively. We report a list of proteins that are reproducibly and significantly increased with TGF-β treatment of fibroblasts and are also found in lavage fluid of bleomycin mouse lungs. Notably, a significant fraction of these proteins is known to bind to FN, identifying a novel “FN-binding protein signature” of IPF. We suggest that this signature may be an important tool for diagnosing and understanding fibrosis in the lung and other tissues.

## Materials and methods

### Cell culture, reagents, and antibodies

Normal human lung fibroblasts (NHLF, Lonza CC-2512) and diseased human lung fibroblasts from idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis patients (DHLF, Lonza CC-7231) were cultured in complete medium, FGM-2 Fibroblast Growth Medium-2 BulletKit (Lonza CC-3132, FBM Basal Medium and FGM-2 supplements). NHLFs and DHLFs were used for experiments through Passage 6. For TGF-β treatment, fibroblasts were seeded in complete medium at a density of 3*104/cm2 and allowed to attach for 6 h followed by overnight starvation in FBM Basal Medium supplemented with 0.1% FBS (Hyclone). Cells were stimulated with TGF-β1 (5 ng/ml) (Peprotech, 100-21) for 6, 24, and 48 h in starvation medium for gene and protein expression studies and in complete medium for matrix assembly experiments.

Antibodies used in this study were mouse monoclonal HFN 7.1 anti-human FN antibody from concentrated supernatant (Developmental Studies Hybridoma Bank, Univ. Iowa), rabbit polyclonal anti-FN antiserum (R184) and rabbit polyclonal anti-TN-C antiserum (R759) [15] (both prepared in-house), rabbit polyclonal anti-FN (Abcam, ab32419), rabbit polyclonal isotype control (Abcam, ab37415), rabbit anti-GAPDH monoclonal antibody (Cell Signaling, 2118), mouse anti-EDA monoclonal antibody (AdipoGen, AG-20B-6001PF-C100), rabbit anti-IGFBP3 monoclonal antibody (Cell Signaling, 13216), and goat anti-IGFBP3 polyclonal antibody (R&D systems, AF775).

### Animals

Male C57BL/6 mice with an average weight of 25-30g were obtained from Jackson Laboratory. Mice were single housed in a temperature-controlled environment (20–24 °C) on 12 h light–dark cycle and provided food and water ad libitum. All animal husbandry and procedures were approved by the Bristol Myers Squibb Company Animal Care and Use Committee and were conducted in conformity with the Public Health Service Policy on Humane Care and Use of Laboratory Animals.

### Intratracheal Bleomycin Mouse Model

Mice were placed in an induction chamber and anesthetized by a mixture of isoflurane delivered in oxygen until a surgical plane of anesthesia was reached which was determined by respiratory rate and toe pinch. The animals were then suspended on an induction board by their incisors and an otoscope and lead wire were used to guide an indwelling catheter (20g x 1in) into the trachea. Once the catheter was in place, the lead wire was removed and a single treatment (PBS or Bleomycin 1 U/kg Sigma lot # 3670656) was administered into the hub of the catheter and passively inspired during normal respiration. Once the total volume (4 ml/kg) was inhaled the catheter was removed and the animals were allowed to recover from anesthesia prior to being returned to the housing room.

Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid was collected 21 d after bleomycin treatment. Mice were anesthetized with an injectable anesthesia mixture (10 mg/ml Ketamine and 0.7 mg/ml Xylazine) administered via IP injection (12.5 ml/kg) until a surgical plane of anesthesia was reached as determined by respiratory rate and toe pinch. A small skin excision was made on the ventral neck region and blunt dissection was used to expose the trachea. The trachea was then catheterized with a luer hub (20g x 0.5in) and secured with suture. A 1ml syringe pre-filled with cold 5 mM EDTA in HBSS was secured to the luer hub and a single wash was performed to collect bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) fluid. BAL fluid was centrifuged (500xg for 8 min in 4 °C) to pellet cells and supernatant was collected for analysis. Mice were then exsanguinated via cardiac puncture. The tracheobronchial tree and lungs were excised with luer hub still sutured in place. A 3 ml syringe pre-filled with 10% neutral buffered formalin (NBF) was attached to luer hub and a volume was delivered until lungs were fully inflated without overdistension. A suture was used to tie off trachea below luer hub and tissues were placed in individual jars pre-filled with 10% NBF.

### Histochemistry

5 µm tissue sections from paraffin embedded mouse lung were processed on the Sakura Tissue Tek Prisma automated tissue stainer using manufacturer recommended protocols for hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining. In brief, xylene was used to dewax the tissue, followed by rehydration with alcohol and water. Hematoxylin was applied to stain nuclei, followed by differentiation reagent. Next, eosin counterstain was used to stain the cytoplasm and extracellular components of the tissue. Alcohol rinses and xylene clearing made the tissue transparent before mounting with a coverslip and mounting media. Slides were left at room temperature to cure before imaging on the Aperio AT2 (Leica Biosystems, Deer Park, IL, USA) whole slide scanner.

For immunohistochemistry, the Bond Polymer Refine detection system (Leica Biosystems, DS9800) was used in the automated staining protocol with the polyclonal rabbit anti-FN antibody. Slides were rinsed in ddH2O prior to mounting with a glass coverslip and brightfield imaging on the Phenoimager HT. Images were exported into HALO v3.4.2986.166 (Indica Labs, Albuquerque, New Mexico, USA) and analyzed using the CytoNuclear and Area algorithms. Single cell positivity and area analysis was graphed using GraphPad Prism v9.5.

Assessment of fibrotic regions was performed using a HALO AI-based classifier called Densenet V2. Alveolar regions of interest were selected in the distal portion of healthy lung sections stained with H&E; these images were annotated as normal and used to train the classifier. Alveolar regions with higher cell density and strong eosin staining outside of the nuclei were selected on lung sections from bleomycin-treated mice and used as fibrotic for classifier training. The classifier was utilized to analyze all of the H&E images from the two groups (2 images per animal). The % of the tissue that was classified as fibrotic or normal is reported.

### Immunoblotting and protein analyses

Conditioned medium (CM) was collected from NHLFs, cells were lysed in deoxycholate (DOC) buffer, DOC-soluble and DOC-insoluble fractions were isolated by centrifugation, and the DOC-insoluble pellet was solubilized in SDS buffer by boiling following the procedures as described [10]. To analyze intracellular FN in sub-confluent cells, NHLFs were stimulated with TGF-β for 48 h, then re-plated at a sub-confluent density for 4 h before lysing in SDS lysis buffer (2% SDS, 20 mM Tris-HCl, pH 8.8, 2 mM EDTA) with protease inhibitor. Total protein concentrations of DOC-soluble and sub-confluent SDS lysates were determined by BCA assay (Pierce). Equal volumes of CM, equal amounts of total protein from SDS lysates or DOC-soluble fractions and proportional volumes of DOC-insoluble samples were separated by SDS-PAGE on 6% (for FN, EDA-FN, TN-C) and 10% (for IGFBP3 and GAPDH) polyacrylamide gels. Gels were transferred to a nitrocellulose membrane and immunoblotted as described [10]. Concentrations of BALF samples were determined by spectrophotometry using A280 (1Abs = 1mg/ml, a general reference setting based on a 0.1% protein solution producing an Absorbance of 1.0 A). BALF samples in control and in fibrotic groups were analyzed by SDS-PAGE and silver staining [16]. The fibrotic BALF samples, diluted 1:10, were analyzed using R184 anti-FN and R759 anti-TN-C antisera at 1:10,000 and 1:2000 dilutions, respectively. Other antibody dilutions were: HFN 7.1 (1:10,000), anti-EDA-FN (1:1000), and both anti-IGFBP3 antibodies (1:1000). Secondary HRP-conjugated antibodies (ThermoFisher Scientific) were used at 1:10,000 dilution. SuperSignal West Pico Plus ECL reagent (Pierce) was used for developing blots. Azure imaging system was used for imaging blots and AzureSpot Pro was used for band density analysis. Band intensities within the linear range were used for quantification.

### Immunofluorescence microscopy

For matrix staining, NHLFs were seeded on glass coverslips and stimulated with TGF-β as described above. After 48 h, NHLFs were fixed with 3.7% formaldehyde in PBS and incubated with anti-FN (R184 at 1:100) or anti-EDA antibody (1:100) followed by Alexa-Fluor-488- or 568-conjugated goat anti-rabbit or goat anti-mouse IgG (Invitrogen,1:500). For intracellular FN staining after TGF-β stimulation, NHLFs were re-seeded at sub-confluence at a density of 0.75*104cells/cm2. After 4-6 h attachment, NHLFs were fixed and permeabilized with 0.5% Triton X-100 in PBS for 15 min at room temperature, followed by staining as above. Samples were mounted in VECTASHIELD Vibrance antifade mounting medium (H-1700). A Nikon Eclipse Ti microscope with a Hamamatsu C10600 ORCA-R2 digital camera was used to capture images. Mean fluorescence measurements were performed using ImageJ on 7 randomly selected fields per condition. Representative fields are shown. Images were adjusted equivalently using ImageJ.

RNA (1 μg) was reversed transcribed using random hexamer primers and qPCR reactions were performed with a Mx3000P QPCR system (Agilent Technologies) using primers listed in table and conditions as described [17]. ### RNA-sequencing and analysis

Duplicated RNA samples in each condition (+/− TGF-β) from each donor were submitted to the Genomics Core Facility at the Lewis Sigler Institute for Integrative Genomics (Princeton University). RNA samples of normalized concentrations were used as input for reverse transcription using barcoded oligo-dT primers to index each cDNA sample following the drop-seq method [18]. The pooled barcoded cDNA samples were purified and amplified by PCR, then turned into sequencing libraries using the Nextera kit (Illumina, CA) to include only the poly-A tail adjacent 3’ ends of the transcripts. The cDNA samples and sequencing libraries were examined on the Bioanalyzer (Agilent, CA) DNA HS chips for size distribution, and quantified by Qubit fluorometer (Invitrogen, CA). The purified library pool was sequenced on Illumina NovaSeq 6000 using the SP 100 cycle kit v1.5. Raw sequencing reads were filtered by Illumina NovaSeq Control Software and only the Pass-Filter (PF) reads were used for further analysis.

FASTQ files generated from above were used to identify the differentially expressed genes. The reads were aligned using STAR [19] on the Human Reference Genome (GRCh38). The transcript abundance estimation was performed using RSEM [20]. The quality of the sequence data was assessed using multiQC v1.12 [21]. Count and TPM data were generated from the pipeline for further analysis and visualizations to identify differentially expressed genes in NHLF cells treated with TGF-β at 48 h. After filtering non-expressed or low-expressed genes based on counts per million (CPM), 24,489 genes with CPM values above 1 remained. Differential Expression analysis was carried out using PyDEseq2 python package [22]. The Matrisome Project website (https://sites.google.com/uic.edu/matrisome/home) contains a tool, Matrisome AnalyzeR (https://matrinet.shinyapps.io/MatrisomeAnalyzer/), that was used to classify our RNA-sequencing gene lists into three groups: non-matrisome, matrisome-associated and core matrisome.

### Luminex analysis

NHLFs were cultured and stimulated as described above in starvation medium. The CM was collected at 48 h and stored with 10 mM EDTA, 2 mM PMSF at −20°C until analyzed. The concentration of soluble protein analytes in CM was measured using a Luminex™ Bead-Based multiplexed assay with commercially available soluble protein analyte panels from Millipore-Sigma (analyte information is listed in Supplementary Table 4). Data were collected using a FLEXMAP 3D™ instrument. Standard curves were derived, and analyte concentrations were calculated with Bio-Plex Manager™ (Bio-Rad) software using phycoerythrin median fluorescence intensity (MFI) data. Ranges of reliable analyte detection are presented in Supplementary Table 4. For FN analyses, cell supernatants were diluted 1:1000 and patient plasma samples were diluted 1:400,000 to bring FN into the range of the assay.

For each biomarker, the concentration values in each group were checked to ensure they were within the lower limit of quantification (LLOQ) and upper limit of quantification (ULOQ). The values that fell outside this range were excluded from further analysis (with a few exceptions for manual check as their values before or after TGF-β treatment drastically changed and fell outside of the thresholds). The remaining values were log2 transformed and normality was assessed using the Shapiro-Wilk test [23] and visual inspection of raw data. Unpaired t-tests were performed to compare the mean concentration values of each biomarker between the comparison groups (such as +/− TGF β). The log2 fold change was calculated between the mean values of each group for each biomarker. All statistical analyses were performed using Python and data visualizations were created using Spotfire (v12) software.

### Statistical analyses

Immunoblot and immunofluorescence results are reported as the mean ± standard error of multiple independent experiments as noted in figure legends. Statistical analyses for experiments with stimulation at a single time point were performed using an unpaired, two tailed Student’s t-test. With stimulation at multiple time points, two-way ANOVA was applied, with p < 0.05 considered statistically significant. RNA-seq and Luminex data statistics were calculated as described above.

## Results

### Effects of TGF-β on fibronectin expression

Normal human lung fibroblasts (NHLFs) derived from donors were shown to respond to TGF-β treatment as expected at both the mRNA and protein levels. TGF-β-dependent changes in FN expression were confirmed by comparing NHLFs either without or treated with TGF-β for 24 and 48 h after serum starvation. Using qPCR, we found that total FN mRNA increased more than 4-fold at 24 h but continued to increase to > 5-fold by 48 h of treatment (Figure 1A, Supplementary Table 1). Results were equivalent with NHLFs from two different donors. Because alternative splicing at the extra domain A (EDA) and extra domain B (EDB) exons of the FN transcript has been suggested to associate with fibrosis [24,25], we used qPCR to measure levels of EDA+ and EDB+ FN transcripts relative to total FN. Our results show higher levels of these splice variants with TGF-β treatment (Figure 1B, C), but the change in each was similar to or less than the change in total FN transcripts (Supplementary Table 1) indicating that these isoforms are not enriched compared to total FN with TGF-β stimulation. We observed a similar pattern of change in total and spliced FNs in our analyses of diseased cells (DHLFs) from two donors (Supplementary Figure 1). Direct comparison shows that total FN mRNA levels expressed by untreated DHLFs were 2-3-fold higher than in untreated NHLFs.

Increased mRNA resulted in higher production of FN protein. Subconfluent NHLF cells were lysed after 48 h with or without TGF-β in starvation medium. When subconfluent, the majority of FN is intracellular and thus a measure of protein production. Quantification of immunoblots showed > 7-fold increases in FN protein for both donors when treated under standard conditions on an uncoated culture surface (Figure 2A). Significantly more FN was also detected intracellularly by immunofluorescence of control and treated cells (Figure 2B). Cell-ECM interactions can affect gene expression and TGF-β activity [8,26] so we also tested a collagen-coated substrate, as type I collagen is known to be upregulated under these culture conditions. Comparison of cells cultured on a collagen coat with an uncoated surface showed a similar level of increase (Figure 2A) indicating that increased collagen is not enhancing the effects of TGF-β.

### Fibronectin matrix assembly in response to TGF-β stimulation

A primary function of FN is to assemble into a fibrillar matrix and excess matrix fibrils are a hallmark of fibrosis. To determine how FN matrix levels are affected by TGF-β treatment, NHLFs were incubated with TGF-β in complete medium with serum, which is needed for efficient matrix assembly. Conditioned medium (CM) from confluent cells collected at 48 h of TGF-β treatment contained > 5-fold more FN than CM from untreated cells (Figure 3A). A deoxycholate (DOC) detergent insolubility assay was used to determine levels of FN fibril formation with and without TGF-β treatment. The DOC-soluble material contains intracellular and cell-associated proteins as well as ECM fibrils that are initially soluble in DOC buffer. Over time, fibrils are irreversibly converted into a DOC-insoluble form; the quantity of these insoluble fibrils is a measure of the level of stable FN matrix. Results show dramatic and significant increases in both DOC-soluble and DOC-insoluble FN matrix (Figure 3A, Supplementary Figure 2A). Immunostaining showed that fibril densities and mean fluorescence intensities are also much higher with TGF-β (Figure 3B, Supplementary Figure 2B). Type I collagen fibrillogenesis was increased in treated cells (Supplementary Figure 3) as expected, as collagens depend on FN fibrils to initiate fibrillogenesis.

EDA+ FN production and incorporation into the matrix were analyzed by immunofluorescence. Mean fluorescence intensities of total matrix FN and EDA+ matrix were 1.5 and ~1.2 fold higher, respectively, in TGF-β treated cultures (Supplementary Figure 4A). Band intensities on immunoblots of DOC-soluble and DOC-insoluble fractions increased with TGF-β treatment for both total FN and EDA+ FN (Supplementary Figure 4C, D), while the accumulation of EDA FN in CM was slightly less than that detected for total FN (see Figure 3) (Supplementary Figure 4B). While EDA+ FN protein levels increase with TGF-β stimulation in secreted and matrix fractions, the EDA+ isoform does not show a disproportionately higher increase than total FN. Therefore, contributions to the fibrotic process of the EDA+ isoform cannot be separated from effects of increases in total FN. EDB+ FN protein levels were too low to be detected in our samples.

### Effects of TGF-β on core matrisome gene expression

To identify global ECM gene expression patterns as well as ECM changes with TGF-β stimulation in NHLFs, RNA-seq analyses were performed. The effects of TGF-β were confirmed by expression of the well-established biomarker of fibrosis, smooth muscle actin (ACTA2), which increased nearly 20-fold (log2FC = 4.31, padj = 2.66E-13). Analysis of the RNA-seq data in Matrisome AnalyzeR [27] identified 206 core matrisome genes. The 80 most highly expressed of the 206 ECM genes, with normalized transcripts per million (TPM) > 1, were further analyzed. Expression of 43 of these 80 genes was significantly changed between control and TGF-β conditions with adjusted p-values < 0.05; expression of 34 genes increased and 9 genes decreased (Figure 4A, Supplementary Table 2). IGFBP3, which is known to be up-regulated by TGF-β and several other soluble factors [28], showed the largest Log2FC of 7.31. RNA-seq expression differences with TGF-β were confirmed using two genes with significant changes (THBS1 and THBS2) and each increased at least two-fold by qPCR (Supplementary Figure 5C, D). Periostin gene (POSTN) expression was also analyzed because it showed a Log2FC of 1.16 with a p-value < 0.05 but padj > 0.05. Our qPCR results show a level of change (~3-fold) similar to the RNA-seq results (2.2-fold) (Supplementary Figure 5E).

In parallel, we tested the expression of a panel of 124 soluble protein analytes using a Luminex immunoassay. Antibodies were included that recognize matrisome proteins and soluble factors (Supplementary Table 4) and CM was analyzed from NHLF cells treated with TGF-β or untreated for 48 h. We found that 38 of the 124 proteins were detected in the NHLF medium, 10 of which are core matrisome proteins (Supplementary Table 3). The levels of 7 of the 10 core matrisome proteins (70%) showed log2FC > 1.0 or < −1.0 and/or p-values < 0.05 with TGF-β treatment (Figure 4B). Six of the proteins increased while TN-C levels decreased compared to the control. Immunoblotting of CM and DOC lysates for IGFBP3 protein showed significant accumulation of protein with TGF-β treatment compared to CM and DOC lysates from untreated cells where IGFBP3 was not detectable (Figure 4C; donor 2 data not shown). The fold-change in IGFBP3 from RNA-seq could not be quantified by qPCR because, as with the protein expression, IGFBP3 mRNA was undetectable in untreated cells. TN-C was also analyzed because this protein has been implicated in the development and progression of fibrosis in a number of tissues, including in lung [29], but showed little change with TGF-β in RNA-seq data and a decrease in CM in the Luminex analysis. We confirmed by immunoblotting that TN-C levels were similar in CM with and without treatment (Supplementary Figure 5A). On the other hand, qPCR results (Supplementary Figure 5B) and analysis of TN-C levels in DOC lysates showed higher levels with TGF-β treatment for NHLFs from both donors (Supplementary Figure 5A; donor 2 data not shown). This difference between CM and the cell layer suggests that the lack of a protein change in CM may be due to excess TN-C being incorporated into the FN matrix. Also of note, the DOC-insoluble matrix contained multiple TN-C bands, especially in the TGF-β treated sample (Supplementary Figure 5A, right), suggesting that DOC-soluble and DOC-insoluble fractions may contain different splice variants of TN-C.

Interestingly, of the 80 core matrisome proteins that increased with TGF-β stimulation in our RNA-seq dataset, 25 (30%) have been shown to bind to FN (Supplementary Table 2). Of these, expression of 14 genes was increased, including POSTN, TNC, and FN1 itself, and 2 were decreased (DCN and FBLN1) with TGF-β (Table 1). Of the 7 core matrisome proteins that changed in the Luminex analysis, only IGFBP-7 has not been shown to bind FN (Supplementary Table 3), while the other 6 are in our FN-binding list from the RNA-seq analysis (Table 1). Other than core matrisome proteins, two of the identified soluble factors in the Luminex assay bind to FN (VEGF [30] and HGF [31]) and two extracellular proteases are known to cleave FN (MMP-9 [32] and cathepsin D [33]). Together, our results identify a set of ECM proteins that are both up-regulated with TGF-β stimulation and are documented binding partners for FN, suggesting the existence of a “FN-binding protein signature” that defines IPF.

For FN binding to promote development of fibrosis, one would expect FN levels to be high prior to up-regulation of its binding partners. To test this, we compared changes in the mRNA levels of FN and several other proteins over time. Our results show that FN levels are high at 6 h and increase significantly at subsequent time points (24 and 48 h) (Figure 5). IGFBP3, THBS1 and 2, POSTN, and TNC RNAs increased over time but never to the level of FN. FN protein was also significantly higher than other proteins in the Luminex assay (data not shown). These time course results indicate that FN matrix levels increase early after TGF-β stimulation, supporting the suggestion that sufficient FN matrix would be present to support deposition of other up-regulated core matrisome proteins. Thus, coordinated up-regulation of FN along with a set of FN-binding proteins could potentially increase the rate of progression and the extent of fibrosis in the lung.

### In vivo changes in ECM protein levels with IPF

To determine the relationship between ECM changes in NHLFs treated with TGF-β and in lung disease, we used a mouse model of IPF in which lung fibrosis is induced by treatment with bleomycin [34]. As fibrosis develops, changes in protein expression and deposition will differ between bleomycin- and control-treated mouse lungs. Excess ECM deposition is clearly detectable in bleomycin lung sections with H&E-positive staining area measurements showing a significant fibrotic region (Figure 6A, B). Immunostaining with anti-FN antibody compared to an isotype-matched control antibody demonstrates a dramatic increase in FN deposition with bleomycin treatment (Figure 6C). Both cell positivity and FN staining area were significantly higher (Figure 6D, E). If increases in protein expression are sufficiently high in the tissue, then secreted proteins may be detectable in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF). We analyzed protein levels in BALF collected 21 days after treatment and found up to 15-fold more total protein mass in BALF after bleomycin treatment (Supplementary Figure 6A). SDS-PAGE followed by silver staining for total protein detection showed dramatically higher levels of proteins in the 50 – 75 kDa range (Supplementary Figure 6B), most likely serum albumin and immunoglobulins from blood leakage. In addition, many higher molecular mass bands were present in the bleomycin-treated samples that were not detected in the saline controls. Excess FN in BALF could be explained by leakage of blood plasma. In fact, Luminex analyses of FN levels in plasma from healthy individuals compared to individuals with interstitial lung disease (ILD) showed that the concentration of FN was 2-fold higher on average in the ILD plasma (Supplementary Figure 6C), similar to a previous report [35]. To confirm that BALF contains not only FN from the blood but also tissue-produced proteins, we examined it for the presence of three ECM proteins that are not normally present in blood (TN-C and type I collagen) or are present at very low levels (IGFBP3). All three of these proteins were very high in BALF from treated mice while little if any protein was detected in control mouse BALF (Figure 6F). Anti-IGFBP3 staining of control and bleomycin-treated lung sections show dramatically higher IGFBP3 in the fibrotic lung ECM (Supplementary Figure 7). We conclude that increased IGFBP3 is deposited in the FN matrix of diseased lungs and that BALF contains tissue-derived proteins that have leaked from fibrotic regions of the lung. Taken together, these results show an overlap between proteins that are increased in the cell culture model with those that accumulate in vivo with lung fibrosis.

## Discussion

As a major contributor to fibrosis, TGF-β enhances production of FN and other ECM molecules. FN forms a foundational ECM, and therefore excess deposition of FN could drive fibrosis through accumulation of other ECM proteins on the FN fibrils. To determine whether FN has a central role in progression of fibrosis, we analyzed FN levels in a mouse model of lung fibrosis and TGF-β stimulated NHLFs in culture. In vivo samples showed elevated FN protein in both soluble and matrix forms and TGF-β-stimulated NHLFs expressed significantly higher amounts of FN mRNA, secreted FN protein, and FN matrix. We also found that FN was increased in IPF patient plasma compared to healthy donors. Together, these findings show that up-regulation of FN is a common theme across these models of lung fibrosis. Gene and protein expression profiling by RNA-seq and Luminex assays, respectively, identified core matrisome and secreted factors that changed with TGF-β treatment of NHLFs, with IGFBP3 being the most highly up-regulated. Several of these ECM proteins were examined in BALF from mouse diseased lungs and found to be dramatically increased. Interestingly, of the NHLF core matrisome genes significantly up-regulated by TGF-β treatment, over 40% (14 out of 34) of the encoded proteins are known to bind to FN suggesting the idea that FN may direct the accumulation of these other core matrisome proteins. We propose that fibrosis progresses through expression of a “FN-binding protein signature” that initiates and propagates excess ECM deposition.

The accumulation of disorganized and insoluble matrix fibrils is the basis for fibrosis. Fibrillogenesis of ECM proteins is a cell-mediated process and a number of molecular mechanisms have been linked to increased assembly, besides up-regulation of expression of major ECM components like FN or collagen and their receptors. For example, chronically high glucose levels activate PKC signaling in kidney cells resulting in increased activity of α5β1 integrin, the receptor responsible for FN matrix assembly [9]. FN assembly is also modulated by lysine acetylation [10], the presence of certain ECM molecules such as TN-C or proteoglycans [17,36,37], changes in ERK and Rho GTPase signaling [38-40], and activity levels of focal adhesion proteins such as FAK and Src [41,42]. Thus, there are numerous mechanisms that can contribute to fibrosis. However, even with activation of intracellular pathways, how excess ECM proteins accumulate rather than turnover is not clear. Some evidence has been provided to suggest that the presence of EDA+ and EDB+ alternatively spliced isoforms of FN have fibrosis-specific roles [25]. However, we found that they increased only in proportion to total FN, but not in excess, making their contributions difficult to parse from the simple increase in FN itself.

In its role as a foundational matrix, increased numbers of FN fibrils would be able to promote excessive ECM deposition of a variety of ECM proteins. In fact, our results show not only increased expression and secretion of FN, but also dramatically more fibrillar FN matrix assembled by cells treated with TGF-β and also in bleomycin-treated mouse lungs. RNA and protein analyses show higher FN production prior to increases in other FN-binding proteins. Relevant to fibrosis, higher levels of FN matrix would then provide more binding sites for the FN-binding core matrisome proteins that are also increased in fibrotic conditions. An example of this role was provided by our analysis of type I collagen which was significantly increased in our RNA-seq dataset and also accumulated in association with FN fibrils in TGF-β-treated NHLFs. In addition to type I collagen, other up-regulated FN-binding proteins are known to take on a fibrillar organization in association with FN matrix, such as thrombospondin-1 [43], fibrillin-1 [44] and TN-C [45].

Unlike FN, collagens, and other fibrillar ECM proteins, IGFBP3 is a small protein and is not a structural component of matrix fibrils, and as expected, we detected it in the DOC-soluble matrix, but not in the DOC-insoluble FN fraction (Y.S, unpublished observations). IGFBP3 does have heparin-binding activity [28] and could bind to heparan sulfate proteoglycans and FN fibrils at the same time, perhaps providing a linkage that might organize fibrils in specific geometries. IGFBP3 was undetectable in both gene and protein expression levels in NHLFs without stimulation, but dramatically increased in response to TGF-β and was also abundant in BALF. IGFBP3 forms a complex with IGF1 [28] and therefore, increased production of both IGFBP3 and FN might have an impact on fibrosis development through increased incorporation of IGF1 into matrix.

Investigation of how up-regulated FN-binding proteins contribute to the progression of fibrosis may elucidate novel targets for diagnosis and treatment. But it is also possible that down-regulation of certain core matrisome proteins might exacerbate fibrosis. Fibulin-1 binds to FN’s heparin-binding domain [46] and we showed that binding to this domain of FN modulates cell-ECM interactions by blocking the binding of syndecan receptors [45,47]. Reducing syndecan-FN interactions affects activation of the intracellular signaling proteins FAK and Rho GTPase [47,48] resulting in decreased FN matrix assembly [47]. Perhaps down-regulation of fibulin-1, or other modulatory ECM proteins, might relieve this inhibitory activity such that cell-mediated assembly can proceed in excess.

## Conclusions

Our studies, using a TGF-β-treated NHLF cell culture model and a bleomycin-treated mouse lung fibrosis model, identify a “FN-binding protein signature” linked to excess ECM deposition in IPF. Both FN expression and FN fibril formation were increased by TGF-β stimulation of NHLFs and these increases were confirmed in tissue sections and BALF samples from fibrotic mouse lungs and blood plasma from IPF patients. RNA-seq and Luminex immunoassay experiments were used to identify up-regulated gene expression and protein secretion, respectively, using stimulated NHLFs. Data analyses identified the core matrisome proteins expressed by these cells and, of these, 14 TGF-β-up-regulated proteins are known to bind to FN. Several of the FN-binding proteins were tested and found to be elevated in BALF. The most highly expressed gene and protein was IGFBP3 which may contribute to fibrosis by localizing IGF1 to the FN matrix. Other proteins in the FN-binding signature have roles in adhesion modulation, matrix structure and stability, and cell-ECM interactions suggesting that this signature participates in multiple processes involved in the progression of fibrosis.

Bernardo Gouveia1,6, Sagar U. Setru 2,6, Matthew R. King3, Aaron Hamlin3, Howard A. Stone 4, Joshua W. Shaevitz 2,5 & Sabine Petry 3

Microtubules are generated at centrosomes, chromosomes, and within spindles during cell division. Whereas microtubule nucleation at the centrosome is well characterized, much remains unknown about where, when, and how microtubules are nucleated at chromosomes. To address these questions, we reconstitute microtubule nucleation from puriﬁed chromosomes in meiotic Xenopus egg extract and ﬁnd that chromosomes alone can form spindles. We visualize microtubule nucleation near chromosomes using total internal reﬂection ﬂuorescence microscopy to ﬁnd that this occurs through branching microtubule nucleation. By inhibiting molecular motors, we ﬁnd that the organization of the resultant polar branched networks is consistent with a theoretical model where the effectors for branching nucleation are released by chromosomes, forming a concentration gradient that spatially biases branching microtbule nucleation. In the presence of motors, these branched networks are ultimately organized into functional spindles, where the number of emergent spindle poles scales with the number of chromosomes and total chromatin area.

Microtubules originate from centrosomes, chromosomes, and spindle microtubules in dividing eukaryotic cells to form mitotic and meiotic spindles. Chromosomal microtubule generation is particularly critical in cells that do not contain centrosomes, such as plant cells and meiotic egg cells in animals1–4. While microtubule nucleation from centrosomes has been well studied, it remains poorly understood how microtubules are generated around chromosomes because spindle microtubules can neither be resolved from one another nor can their exact origins be determined in cells. Thus, it remains a fundamental question in cell biology to understand where, when, and how microtubules are nucleated at chromosomes to build a spindle that successfully captures and segregates chromosomes during cell division. Experiments in meiotic Xenopus laevis egg extracts have demonstrated that chromatin alone can generate spindles and tune a

spindle’s size and shape5–7. Though revelatory, in lieu of actual chromosomes these studies used bacterial DNA on beads to form chromatin beads, which have different shapes and different amounts of chromatin compared to bona ﬁde chromosomes. The studies also lacked kinetochores, the landing pads on chromosomes where microtubules that make up kinetochore ﬁbers bind before pulling sister chromatids apart. Indeed, experiments in cultured mitotic cells have shown that microtubules also form in the vicinity of kinetochores during prometaphase8–15, and in later stages at kinetochores on chromosomes unattached to existing spindle microtubules, as well as far away from the spindle equator, suggesting a back-up mechanism to capture unaligned chromosomes11,12. The chromatin-bound guanine nucleotide exchange factor RCC1 equips Ran with GTP. RanGTP then releases spindle assembly factors (SAFs) sequestered by importin proteins, allowing SAFs to promote microtubule nucleation around chromosomes, as has been shown in Xenopus egg extracts using chromatin beads17 or sperm chromatin18–22, and in mitotic cells23. Cytoplasmic RanGAP1 deactivates RanGTP in a spatially uniform manner24. This combination of a localized source and homogeneous degradation creates RanGTP and SAF gradients centered at chromosomes. A critical SAF is the protein TPX225, which along with the protein complex augmin, the γ-tubulin ring complex (γ-TuRC), and XMAP215, promotes the nucleation of new microtubules from the surface of existing microtubules26. This process, known as branching microtubule nucleation, generates the majority of spindle microtubules in mitotic cells27 and Xenopus egg extracts28. Yet, where exactly branching microtubule nucleation occurs around chromosomes remains an open question. There could be other microtubule nucleation pathways at play that originate from chromosomes. For example, the chromosomal passenger complex (CPC) at the centromeres of chromosomes29 promotes microtubule growth by inhibiting the microtubule depolymerase MCAK, thereby promoting microtubule polymerization in Xenopus egg extracts30. It was shown that spindles can assemble around sperm nuclei in a manner independent of RanGTP but that requires the CPC31. The degree to which chromosomal microtubule nucleation differentially depends on RanGTP and the CPC, and whether branching microtubule nucleation occurs, remain to be determined. Lastly, most quantitative studies to date have focused only on how microtubule nucleation sustains the steady-state metaphase spindle28,32–34, but do not address the question of how a spindle builds its microtubule network starting from scratch at the end of interphase. Similarly, simulations have focused on either the steady-state metaphase spindle32 or how centrosomes search for and capture kinetochores35,36. Currently, no quantitative model that starts with a realistic initial condition exists to describe how microtubules nucleate from chromosomes in the early stages of acentrosomal spindle assembly. To explore these questions, we combine experiments that reconstitute microtubule nucleation from puriﬁed chromosomes in meiotic Xenopus egg extract with a mathematical model of branching nucleation in a SAF gradient. By directly visualizing microtubule nucleation at chromosomes using totalinternal reﬂection ﬂuorescence microscopy (TIRFM), we reveal where individual microtubules nucleate, at what distances and orientations with respect to chromosomes they form, and how this is inﬂuenced by the amount of chromatin and the number of chromosomes. By comparing experimental results to our model, we ﬁnd that SAF-mediated branching microtubule nucleation in the vicinity of chromosomes provides the main source of microtubules for acentrosomal spindles in Xenopus egg extract. We then establish how the structures of functional spindles that selforganize around puriﬁed chromosomes change with the amount of chromatin and the number of chromosomes.

Results Microtubule-dependent microtubule nucleation is initiated near chromosomes It is challenging to directly visualize the nucleation of individual microtubules near chromosomes in cells because the spindle becomes dense with microtubules within minutes7,37,38. To overcome this obstacle, we reconstituted chromosomal microtubule nucleation ex vivo. Brieﬂy, we puriﬁed mitotic chromosomes with kinetochores labeled with GFP-CENPA from cultured mitotic HeLa cells. To enable

live visualization of individual microtubules nucleating and growing at the onset of spindle assembly, we attached puriﬁed, DAPI-stained chromosomes to the functionalized and passivated glass coverslip of a microscope ﬂow chamber (“Methods”). We then added Xenopus egg extract supplemented with ﬂuorescent tubulin and EB1 to label microtubules and their growing plus-ends, respectively (Fig. 1a). The action of molecular motors was inhibited using the drug vanadate. Using 4-color time-lapse TIRFM, we observed polar microtubule networks forming near chromosomes (Fig. 1b, Supplementary Movie 1, and Supplementary Fig. S1). When the extract solution was ﬁrst added to surface-bound chromosomes, a small number of microtubules in the extract nucleated de novo, i.e., independent of chromosomes, and were visible at low density throughout the imaging ﬁeld regardless of whether a chromosome was nearby (Supplementary Fig. S2a). When a de novo microtubule randomly happened to reach the vicinity of a chromosome, microtubules started to nucleate from it. These newly nucleated microtubules then served as seeds that nucleated more microtubules along them, leading to the formation of a microtubule network of uniform polarity (Fig. 1b, Supplementary Figs. S1 and S2b, and Supplementary Movie 1), similar to the networks observed in previous studies of branching microtubule nucleation26,39. In total, 50% of these early nucleation events occurred within 4 μm of a kinetochore and 55% of these nucleated microtubules grew at an angle less than 40° with respect to the kinetochore (Fig. 1c). These results demonstrate that most microtubule nucleation in this system is microtubuledependent, i.e., it requires a de novo microtubule template to catalyze the formation of the eventual network. Furthermore, microtubule nucleation is ampliﬁed near and directed toward the kinetochores of isolated mitotic chromosomes.

Branching microtubule nucleation is the principal source of chromosomal microtubules Is branching microtubule nucleation indeed the principal source of chromosomal microtubule nucleation observed in Fig. 1? In order to assess this question, we individually immunodepleted the essential Xenopus branching factors TPX2 and augmin from the extract26 and performed the TIRFM assay (Fig. 2a). In control experiments, using a random IgG antibody for immunodepletion, 34 ± 26% of chromosome clusters generated microtubule networks (n = 27 ﬁelds totaling 213 clusters) (Fig. 2a, left). In contrast, we rarely saw microtubule networks generated at chromosomes after depletion of either augmin or TPX2 (Fig. 2a middle and right, Supplementary Fig. S3, and Supplementary Movies 2 and 3). Less than 1 ± 2% of chromosome clusters for either augmin depletion or for TPX2 depletion generated microtubule networks (n > 10 ﬁelds per condition, with >135 clusters per condition) (Fig. 2b). These results suggest that branching microtubule nucleation, mediated by augmin and TPX2, is the key pathway to generate microtubules from chromosomes in Xenopus egg extracts. Therefore, in meiotic Xenopus egg extract spindles, chromosomal microtubule nucleation and branching microtubule nucleation are one and the same, and are the origin of the majority of early spindle microtubules.

By deriving an explicit formula, we see that their system corresponds to Eq. (1) when B = 1. If B > 1, branching microtubule nucleation outcompetes microtubule turnover, and an autocatalytic branched network forms that can propagate indeﬁnitely (Fig. 3f). We ﬁnd that our experimentally measured plus-end distribution (Fig. 3c, left) is well described by our theory with B = 1.7 (Fig. 3c, middle) during the autocatalytic growth phase. After autocatalytic growth, the plus-end distribution reaches a statistically stationary state that is still consistent with B > 1 organization. If saturation were due to increasing microtubule turnover, the organization of the plus-end distribution would have to change to that predicted by B < 1, which we do not observe experimentally. Therefore, we attribute the reason for network saturation as owing to a limited pool of nucleating factors, and not to increasing microtubule turnover.

Analysis of bulk spindle organization in Xenopus egg extract Because the puriﬁed chromosomes are immobilized to the coverslip, they are prevented from rearranging to accommodate the forces from motors, leading to spindle poles that are less stable (Fig. 5b and Supplementary Movie 6). By imaging in the TIRF ﬁeld, we additionally cannot observe poles that might form above the coverslip. Also, our TIRFM assays were performed using DAPI-stained chromosomes, which might interfere with DNA resulting in less robust spindles. To overcome these issues, we incubated unstained chromosomes in bulk extract and allowed spindles to form in a three-dimensional environment. After 45 min, samples were diluted and spin-mounted onto coverslips, after which they were chemically ﬁxed and immunostained for proteins involved in spindle self-organization and for chromatin. Each structure was imaged as a z-stack using epiﬂuorescence microscopy (“Methods”). Just as in the TIRFM assay, we observed multipolar structures organized around chromosomes (Fig. 6a, b), where the bipolar spindles now display a robust ellipsoidal shape (Supplementary Fig. S6a). We immunostained for NuMA (Nuclear Mitotic Apparatus), the adapter for cytoplasmic dynein that allows it to bind microtubules and cluster them at their minus ends, forming spindle poles44. As expected, NuMA displayed sharp polar localization (Fig. 6a and Supplementary Fig. S6a), allowing us to unambiguously identify and count functional poles. We also stained for Eg5 (kinesin-5), the tetrameric motor that slides antiparallel microtubules apart to promote poleward ﬂux45,46. We found that Eg5 localized to the entire spindle with enrichment at the poles (Fig. 6b), in agreement with previous measurements on Xenopus egg extract metaphase spindles47. A negative control random IgG showed no signiﬁcant or distinct localization to the spindle (Supplementary Fig. S6b). These results conﬁrm that our reconstituted system can form proper spindles with the correct motor localizations. Over 50% of all imaged spindles (n = 173) were properly bipolar (Fig. 6c). Because our reconstituted system can generate a wide distribution of chromosome cluster sizes with labeled kinetochores, we asked if the resultant spindle polarity scaled with the chromatin area or number of chromosomes. We found that both increasing chromatin area and the number of chromosomes lead to an increasing number of poles (Fig. 6d, e). This is consistent with a recent study that showed that increasing amounts of branching nucleation can stabilize an

additional spontaneously formed pole48. Interestingly, single chromosomes were only capable of generating monopoles (Fig. 6e), suggesting that there is a minimum number of chromosomes required for the organization of a proper bipolar spindle.

Discussion In this work, we report experimental and theoretical advances to investigate acentrosomal spindle assembly in Xenopus laevis egg extracts, and can now propose the following model (Fig. 6f). First, de novo microtubules nucleate randomly throughout the cytoplasm. When one of the microtubules ﬁnds its way near chromosomes, branched microtubules nucleate from it due to the action of the RanGTP-mediated SAF gradient around chromosomes. In the absence of motors, branched microtubule networks of uniform polarity directed toward chromosomes form (Figs. 1 and 4). When motors are present, self-organized multipolar microtubule networks form around chromosomes (Figs. 5 and 6). It is important to discuss other systems where the mechanism of acentrosomal spindle assembly is different from our model. For example, previous work in mouse oocytes showed that multiple small microtubule organizing centers (MTOCs) with pericentrin-rich poles consisting of many microtubules coalesce and seed the subsequent Ran-dependent assembly of spindle mass after the breakdown of the nuclear envelope49. Whether chromosomes contribute to this Randependent assembly, by releasing factors that enable branching nucleation, remains to be determined. In meiosis I, as opposed to the meiosis II arrested extract we study here, early spindle assembly initiates near the disassembling nuclear envelope in C. elegans50 and is independent of RanGTP in mice and Xenopus oocytes51. Thus, acentrosomal spindle assembly in meiosis I is biophysically distinct from that in meiosis II. Previous work suggested that microtubules formed at random locations and orientations at the start of meiotic spindle assembly, based on imaging techniques that could not resolve individual ﬁlaments6,37,45. In contrast, because TIRFM provides excellent signal-tonoise ratio, we see that single de novo microtubules seed the formation of branched microtubules that are no longer randomly oriented, but rather nucleate near and are directed towards chromosomes, which we attribute to the spatial bias generated by the SAF gradient. Consequently, the capture of chromosomes by the spindle during meiosis in Xenopus is made more likely. How kinetochores are efﬁciently captured and kinetochore ﬁbers form in both centrosomal and acentrosomal systems is a key question in cell biology. Our results show one pathway for acentrosomal spindle assembly uses polarized, branched networks that point toward chromosomes due to a spatially biasing SAF gradient. A recent study27 lends support to this idea, as it was found in human mitotic cells that microtubules nucleated towards kinetochores in an augmindependent manner, and that this process is essential for kinetochore ﬁber maintenance during metaphase. We note that our model does not require nor suggest that kinetochores themselves speciﬁcally stimulate branching nucleation, but rather relies only on the ability of chromatin-bound RCC1 to produce RanGTP to release SAFs in a gradient around chromosomes. This contrasts with other proposed mechanisms whereby kinetochores themselves can either recruit γTuRC directly via the Nup107–160 nucleoporin14 or recruit pericentrin to their transient ﬁbrous corona52, both of which allow for microtubule nucleation directly from kinetochores. It might be that these pathways play a supporting role in our system. To know for certain would require performing additional TIRFM assays with chromosomes lacking kinetochores and isolated kinetochores and comparing the resulting microtubule networks. In our system, branching microtubule nucleation is spatially regulated by a RanGTP-mediated SAF gradient (Fig. 4). Indeed, we explicitly showed that this was the case for TPX2 (Fig. 4b), a known SAF

Such future studies would help further rationalize the novel scaling relationships we report in Fig. 6d, e. These issues are starting to be quantitatively addressed64–66, with the ultimate goal being to minimally reconstitute a functional acentrosomal spindle in vitro.
